As the Superintendent-President Dr. Mike Muñoz is the chief executive officer of the district and oversees the Long Beach City College (LBCC) administration. Nationally recognized as a transformational leader, Dr. Muñoz led LBCC since March 4, 2021. As the Superintendent-President Dr. Mike Muñoz is the chief executive officer of the district and oversees the Long Beach City College (LBCC) administration. Nationally recognized as a transformational leader, Dr. Muñoz led LBCC since March 4, 2021. He is an expert in closing racial equity gaps for students of color, creating inclusive campus cultures for LGBTQIA+ students, and efficiently executing innovative change that makes LBCC a destination college for students from all backgrounds.

A first-generation college student, Dr. Muñoz is a product of the California Community College system, attending East Los Angeles College and Fullerton College before transferring to the University of California, Irvine, where he received his Bachelor of Arts in Psychology and Social Behavior. He received Master of Arts degree in Counseling and his Doctorate of Education with a specialization in Community College Leadership, from California State University, Long Beach. While attending college, he experienced both food and housing insecurity — all while caring for his daughter as a single father.

Dr. Muñoz has extensive experience teaching both at the undergraduate and graduate levels in counseling and higher education. He has taught master’s level courses at California State University, Long Beach, and USC, and doctoral level courses at California State University, Los Angeles. He’s currently serving as an Adjunct Professor of Higher Education at the USC Rossier School of Education teaching a leadership course focused on Community Colleges. Dr. Muñoz was recognized as an Outstanding Faculty Member in 2019 by USC’s Rossier Student Organization, and the 2018 Dr. Cynthia S. Johnson Award from CSULB for his contributions to higher education through exceptional student mentoring. The Los Angeles Times honored Dr. Muñoz by including him in their “L.A. Influential” list in 2024, recognizing him as a “College champion of marginalized students.”

excerpts.line: Transferability & Articulation - Long Beach City College
window: Transferability & Articulation - Long Beach City College
Courses intended to support student transfer should be developed with transferability and articulation in mind from the beginning. These concepts are related, but they are not the same.

A course may be transferable without having a specific articulation agreement, and being transferable does not automatically mean that a course satisfies major preparation, General Education, or C-ID requirements. LBCC describes articulation as the formal process through which courses are evaluated for how they apply at receiving institutions.

Articulation goes beyond determining whether units transfer. It establishes how an LBCC course may satisfy requirements at another institution. An articulation agreement may establish that a course satisfies:
Course-to-Course Articulation — An LBCC course is accepted in place of a specific course at a university.
Major Preparation — The course satisfies a lower-division requirement for a particular major.

The Articulation Officer is an important partner in the C-ID process. The Articulation Office also coordinates the formal submission of eligible LBCC courses for C-ID review.

Research Before You Write the COR
Faculty can significantly improve the likelihood of successful transfer and articulation review by conducting research before the Course Outline of Record is finalized.

Start by examining several comparable courses rather than copying a single university COR. Look for common expectations across institutions and consider how they relate to the course LBCC intends to offer. Pay particular attention to:
Units & Hours — Are the units reasonably consistent with comparable courses?
Prerequisites — Do receiving institutions expect students to enter with particular preparation?

window: Course Content — Does the COR include the breadth and depth expected within the discipline?
Objectives & Outcomes — Do they reflect an appropriate level of collegiate rigor?
Assignments & Evaluation — Does the expected student work demonstrate the academic preparation necessary for subsequent coursework?

ASSIST is the official repository of articulation for California’s public colleges and universities.​
California’s Official Articulation Repository ASSIST is a computerized student-transfer information system that can be accessed at www.assist.org.​
